claims.text: The onset and progression of the phase transition in solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles is governed by defect-induced surface premelting.
Rapid Joule heating generates a high density of surface defects in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Surface defects act as nucleation sites for a transient liquid-like layer.
The surface liquid-like layer propagates inward and enables complete melting.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are solid, disordered solid solutions with relatively uniform composition.
Joule heating permits precise control of temperature and heating and cooling rates.
Relevant rapid-heating treatments can span tens of milliseconds to several minutes.
Rapid cooling on the order of 10^4 K/s can preserve a nanoparticle structure after heating.
Rapid Joule heating produces thermal gradients and stresses in the nanoparticles.
Surface defects lower the local melting barrier and local melting temperature.
Continued heating causes surface liquid regions to coalesce and advance toward the nanoparticle interior.
Rapid quenching freezes intermediate structures so that the transition pathway can be observed experimentally.
A liquid-like surface layer should appear before full melting under rapid Joule heating.
Nanoparticles with higher initial defect density should exhibit a lower premelting onset temperature.
Nanoparticles with higher initial defect density should progress to complete melting faster.
Lower-defect nanoparticles should have a higher, more spatially uniform melting onset without marked surface premelting.
Slow heating may anneal defects sufficiently that defect-induced surface premelting no longer dominates.
Substrate interactions may alter defect dynamics enough to invalidate the proposed mechanism.
The quantitative relationship between surface-defect density and local melting-point depression is not established.
Equivalent premelting onset temperatures and progression behavior in high- and low-defect samples would falsify the hypothesis.
